entry.title: Manila
entry.content:
Here I am, in Manila. My hotel residence is in the north part of town just before the big concentration starts to thin towards the jungle hills. It rains constantly, through sunshine and dark nights. It is a pleasant, warm rain that does not disturb nor slow the constant traffic outside my window. Life continues apace no matter the hour. In fact, when I wander out shortly before midnight to take the metro to some errand, the dank station tunnels are filled with a zoo of workers and revelers elbowing past each other to make the next upcoming train. The pipes hanging above, snaking their way through the station are covered in what is hopefully moss, but probably mold.

The train is obviously going the wrong way, for some reason I can’t fathom, taking me further into the city center. I guess my errand was outside the city. It is unclear how I know what direction I originally intended.

I exit the station to street level, standing underneath opressive advertisements eclipsing the entire facades of apartment buildings. Backfiring mopeds and scooters buzz by. What looks like a rider mower is doing donuts in the intersection. On one side of the tractor is an American flag; presumably this is a John Deere, not like I know many other tractor brands (volvo?). A few kids are riding the mower, probably having a ton of fun.

entry.title: Meteor
entry.content:
There was definitely something bad coming, like a meteor/asteroid. It was imminent and certain to strike near where some friends and I had holed up. The mood could only be described as ambivalent, since there was no screaming or frantic energy in the face of certain doom. I recall we were in a trench with a portrusion of concrete and soil jutting out right overhead. We took our position right before impact; it is not clear how we knew what time impact was expected but we did.

First it was quiet and still after the main collision. There was no flash of light or anything cinematicly epic about our view. We could only look out, past the direction the impacts debris were expected to travel. We had our back to the bomb. Seconds after impact, we saw the refuse and projectiles kicked up from the collision flying by like organic missiles. It was a sideways rain of shear forced earth jetison which we were powerless to do nothing but watch. It seemed like an unspoken truth that death could have come at any moment and squashed our crag halo, but alas everything settled after not too long. The heat of astral trash warmed our heads as we emerged.

entry.title: Midterms
entry.content:
Okay, yeah a week late and everyone has blasted their thoughts about the midterms out. Like a lot of people I know, I spent a good chunk of my waking hours on midterm Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning refreshing the increasingly filled in map of the US house and senate results. The hashed outlines of states yet to be filled in soon became bluer and bluer. The vast swath of American land was by Thursday an azure expanse. Governors, state houses, clerks, the whole gammut. There was a palpable sigh of relief that some abstract collection of things were going to change, but this time in a good direction.

The relief is real, but fleeting. I am glad that Greg Abbott is leaving office. I am glad that Vivek Ramaswamy wont hold office. I’m elated that Annie Andrews decesively won in South Carolina. I’m sort of in disbelief that Cyndie Hyde-Smith is on her way out in Mississipi. But the force of the electorate feels to have been saying something similar each election: life is getting worse, and the people in charge arent steering things effectively. We are still in an anti-incumbancy period, and it’s a mistake to think next election voters will be more lenient towards those that do not act.

The diagnosis of why Republicans did so poorly is not hard to figure out. Trump and many Republicans won in 2024 because life was getting worse and more expensive. Hope was scarce. Winning in 2024 was rarely a reflection of policy choices you as a candidate were vouching for. The assumption the winners of 2024 made was that their ideas were what broke through to normal people. I am highly dubious of the assumption here. Likewise, I am dubious of the people who think they won in 2026 because of their ideas. Don’t get me wrong, I am in favor of medicare-for-all, abortion access, and logical immigration reform. But the winner of 2026 tended to be the person against Data Centers, against masked agents in the street abducting our neighbors.

The next step after winning feels improbably hard to me, an armchair observer of politics. We are in a mess, and due for a reckoning. I fear it is time we start eating our vegetables, and take the wellfare of our countrymen gravely seriously. I dont think that requires taking down the economy at large, but things will probably need to slow before they accelerate again. Or maybe not.

The most unambiguously good thing to come out of the 2026 cycle was how limited cultural politics seemed to be in effective campaigns. My as of now largely unbaked idea is the use of cultural politics as an escape hatch from politicking on issues that affect people at a ycore level. Trans bathroom issues can rile people up in certain states, but riling people up on the same old crud can only work for so many campaigns before people realize that they too are engaging in a world poorer, less imaginative, and more stuck then the progress of their early years. And that is how Mississippi goes blue, and then back to red, and then blue again.

I expect the colors to strobe for a while, until we start making good progress.

entry.title: Drive East
entry.content:
Was on a drive east with N*. We were rolling around banks of big deciduous trees, standing tall and slanting slightly over the highway bends. The sky was steel grey and full, the clouds straining like a pillowcase filled with water about to rip through the cloth. We had a nice convo about this and that. Could not for the life of me remember what any topic was. If memory serves we were deep in tennessee, ripping up through stubborn apalachia valley land.

We had to stop for the night. Some tall quarry tower served as the rendezvous point for some union outfit. These workers were all women in overalls, grease stained and muddy. No idea how but we two boys had infiltrated their session and were takin is as equals. We laughed, though did not ask what they were up to. There was a jolly spirit in the air.

entry.title: Snack Shack
entry.content:
I had a great one the other night. It was so good I woke up right afterwards, around 3am, and told myself to jot down the notes in my phone. Alas, I continued to sleep and after waking up from my alarm, making coffee, and feeding scooty nearly everything I dreamt of had vanished from memory.

From what I remember, I certainly was at a snack shack with my friend JJ. A snack shack is, from what I remember of days in the Rio Grande Valley, a palace of junk food and sugary drinks. I really don’t think I’ve ever set foot in one, so this is all from vibe and predjudice.

We sat in the snack shack, having a nice time chatting and shooting the breeze. And that’s it. Again, there was a lot more that happened afterwards. I can picture the sky and the ribbons of blue, red, and orange stretched taught towards the western horizon. But yeah, that’s all I got today.

entry.title: 13th Street
entry.content:
It was the end of a relationship, but with M* not C*. Summertime in Austin as we drove through town with the car glass radiating heat shimmers. I had dropped her off I guess as I was soon driving alone. I was caught up in thought of “what am I going to do now”. I thought of what people would think, but I was mostly caught up in the crash of loneliness soon to come as I would have to, sooner or later, face a night in with no one around. No one to bounce ideas off of, no one to catch my porous mind. No one to listen to about the triviality of day to day living.

I drove down 13th st at midday. The world was completely washed out and a sickly grey yellow tone.

entry.title: Hot Tub
entry.content:
At some point of some kind of bachelor or birthday party, I go to take a splash in the hot tub. We were in what could be mistaken for one of those Costa Rican cloud jungle bungalos. It was a fairly tame party all things considered. In fact, it may have even been my bachelor party, in that everyone was there to celebrate me. But the faces and people felt unfamiliar to me, like it was week two of freshman year of college; I know who you are, but I don’t know you in any real sense.

I was feeling ill, or maybe just slightly nauteous. I guess we had been drinking quite a bit. I sit down in the hot tub I guess to relax and help my body shed some toxins. Well shed it did, as I look down and some yellowish brown detritus clouds the bottom of the hot tub. Should I also mention that everyone was in the hot tub. Well they were. I notice the cloud immediately, and try to conceal it by sitting on it using some maneuver to inflate my swim trunks so as to trap the substance the way fireman throw a blanket over a small inferno.

Everyone who noticed it was kind enough not to yelp or draw attention to it. Slowly one-by-one the participants of the hot tub session evacuated to their corridors for what I presume to take a shower. I remain in the hot tub, not willing to unstake my tent so to speak and let out the embarresing evidence of my body breaking down.

entry.title: Ennui
entry.content:
The word of the decade is ennui. The feeling of oppressive boredom which grips any motivation or actionable feeling in a death vice seems like a shared, lingering, global sensation. It is not AI’s fault. It is not climate change’s fault. It is not economic immobility’s fault.

Perhaps it is an all of the above situation. But for now, I will focus on AI. Evidence suggests the big lab’s frontier models are capable of solving or at least expanding our understanding of elusive mathematics problems, problems that have plagued and enticed budding mathematicians for years. Firing up a swarm of agents to iterate on a problem, given nearly infinite funding and compute, seems like it does “something” towards mathematic progress. I’m not a mathematician. For kicks, I took a look at one of the resulting papers of a proof and could not reason anything past the abstract.

Given I’m not a mathematician, the following is pure conjecture. I’d imagine the feeling of a mathematician toiling away for years, getting degrees based on solving a particular proof, delivering lectures and writing endless words on some niche graph theory subject becomes a white whale. The problem becomes the point of life, the goal of being able to push humanity’s collective understanding of the world just a smidge past the high watermark becomes one of the reasons to get out of bed. Sure, there is some hubris involved to be able to attach one’s name to history. But ego has led man to create amazing, beautiful objects to which we are all indebted.

Why then, would I, a supposed mathematician, continue to strive if some nameless swarm of agents can put their nom de plume on the white whale problem, hundreds at a time. What then is the point? Maybe the frontier labs’ goal is to rid humanity of our collective egos; good luck with that. With ego replaced with toil and rote, we can get back to just work. But if there is nothing to which we eventually can claim fame to, we get ennui. We get bored. We ask ourselves what’s the point.

entry.title: Barrow
entry.content:
Found myself somewhere near if not exactly in Barrow, Alaska on the state’s north shore. It was during the summer, where the air was breezy and comfortable, almost unnoticeable. There is a town, or maybe was a town. All the squat tiny concrete homes were boarded up with no sign of recent habitation. I could peek in throuh the shutters and see almost nothing save for a scant couch.

Then suddenly I popped up on the back of a moving golf cart, being driven by someone presumably. I took my flip phone out and started recording a little kitty that had begun following us as we wove around the streets of barrow. The cat was able to keep up with ease. Superstition by Stevie Wonder played in the background.

I continued walking and found a coastal restaurant heavily adorned with those plastic wall leaves most commonly found on touristy cheap restaurants in Europe. Colette and I got a table easily as there was no one else there. There was a vegetarian friendly menu, which surprised us. I got orange chicken.
